Telecom operators are increasingly adopting equipment reuse and refurbishment to reduce network investment costs, limit waste and cut emissions as the industry faces pressure to meet its net-zero target by 2050. The shift is moving operators away from the traditional practice of replacing equipment during network upgrades towards extending the lifespan of existing infrastructure, according to a Research Analyst at GSMA Intelligence, Muskan Gadodia. In an article published on the GSMA website, Gadodia reported that the world’s 10 largest mobile network operators by subscriber base had introduced or supported more than 500 unconventional sustainability initiatives since 2020, either independently or through partnerships. She identified equipment reuse, energy management, smarter procurement, redesigned network sites, environmental restoration and community clean-energy partnerships as six areas in which operators were expanding their sustainability efforts beyond conventional measures. Under the equipment reuse approach, Telefónica’s MAIA platform and Orange’s OSCAR programme are helping to extend the lifespan of network equipment through reuse and refurbishment. The development is also drawing equipment manufacturers into operators’ sustainability programmes. Orange’s OSCAR programme, for instance, has established a formal refurbishment partnership with Nokia, reflecting the growing role of suppliers in efforts to extend the useful life of telecommunications infrastructure. Gadodia said achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 remained one of the industry’s biggest challenges, despite operators’ investments in network efficiency and renewable energy. Most mobile network operators are pursuing this goal through traditional measures such as improving network energy efficiency and increasing the use of renewable energy,” the analyst wrote. Those measures alone might not be sufficient to close the industry’s remaining emissions gap, prompting operators to explore additional initiatives involving infrastructure, energy management and environmental restoration. The analysis also highlighted efforts to turn telecommunications infrastructure into energy assets. Finland’s Elisa is using backup batteries at base stations in a virtual power plant model to support electricity grid balancing, while Deutsche Telekom is deploying waste heat from network facilities. Other operators are incorporating environmental considerations into procurement decisions. Telefónica, for example, has introduced internal carbon pricing into its procurement processes, taking into account energy consumption, emissions and lifetime operating costs alongside purchase prices. In Africa, Airtel Africa’s lean-site model in Nigeria was cited as an example of how operators are redesigning network infrastructure to reduce operational requirements. Japan’s NTT DOCOMO also operates a self-powered hydropower base station. The sustainability drive extends to environmental monitoring and community energy projects. Orange Business and Tēnaka are collaborating on coral reef monitoring, while Vodafone has an environmental monitoring initiative in Scotland. In Kenya, Safaricom’s partnership with Sistema.bio is helping farmers access biodigesters through mobile-enabled payments and loyalty mechanisms. The GSMA’s Mobile Net Zero report showed that the mobile industry’s operational emissions fell by eight per cent between 2019 and 2023, even as data traffic quadrupled. However, the industry needs to reduce emissions by 7.5 per cent annually by 2030, more than twice the average annual rate achieved so far, to reach net zero by 2050. Gadodia said the unconventional initiatives were designed to complement, rather than replace, network modernisation and renewable energy adoption, as operators seek to reduce emissions across their wider operations and supply chains.
